title: The Air India Crash Probe Just Entered Its Final Stage. The Families of 260 Victims Say They Are Still Being Kept in the Dark.
excerpt: Investigators have prepared a cockpit voice recorder transcript and conducted a psychological autopsy. A draft report is expected in October. Meanwhile, families allege they are being pressured to waive legal claims against Boeing.
body:
More than a year after an Air India Boeing 787 crashed shortly after takeoff from Ahmedabad, killing 260 people in the world's deadliest air disaster in a decade, the investigation is finally entering its closing chapter — and the families left behind are running out of patience.

A court filing dated Tuesday revealed that India's Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau has prepared a cockpit voice recorder transcript, conducted a psychological autopsy, and moved into the analysis phase of its probe. A draft final report is expected around October, after which it will be sent to the U.S. National Transportation Safety Board and other participating countries for review before publication.

The disclosures came not through a voluntary update, but through a lawsuit filed by the father of the flight's captain.

## What the Investigators Have Done

The AAIB said it has interviewed Air India 787 pilots, crew members who had previously flown with the pilots of the crashed aircraft, technical personnel involved in preparing the jet, air traffic controllers, weather officials, and human-factors specialists. The families of the flight crew were also approached at their residences during the early stages of the investigation.

An analysis of data retrieved in late May from an engine monitoring unit is still outstanding, and an assessment of "certain organisational factors" remains in progress. The bureau estimated that remaining investigative activities would be completed within about six weeks, subject to "external dependencies."

The filing did not identify whose psychological autopsy was conducted or share any findings.

## A Father's Fight for Answers

The court filing exists because Pushkar Raj Sabharwal, the father of the captain, sued after AAIB officials visited his home and implied that his son had deliberately cut fuel to the plane's engines after takeoff.

A preliminary report released last year showed the Boeing 787's engine fuel control switches moved almost simultaneously from "RUN" to "CUTOFF," starving both engines of fuel shortly after the aircraft left the runway. According to U.S. officials' early assessment reported by Reuters, the cockpit recording of the dialogue between the two pilots supported the view that the captain cut the fuel flow.

The AAIB said at the time it was "too early to reach any definite conclusions." In Tuesday's filing, the bureau noted that media speculation and narratives attributing blame to the pilots had caused some witnesses to become "restrictive and non-responsive" — a rare acknowledgment that premature public judgment was actively hindering the investigation.

## Families Push Back on Compensation Terms

The investigation is not the only battleground. Nearly 30 families have sent a letter to Union Civil Aviation Minister Ram Mohan Naidu outlining five demands: regular updates from the AAIB every 15 to 30 days, independent simulator validation tests before the final report is issued, a clear timeline for the report's release, the inclusion of a seasoned Boeing 787 pilot with crash investigation experience on the probe team, and assurance that families will not be pressured to waive their legal rights.

The last point is the most contentious. Families have alleged that Air India is asking next of kin to sign release documents that would waive legal claims not only against the airline, but also against Boeing, General Electric, GE Aerospace, Safran, and Honeywell — the companies that made the aircraft's airframe, engines, and key systems.

"Families should not be pressured to give up their legal rights before the Final Investigation Report is released and before the full facts are known," one family member wrote.

Air India has said the wording in its compensation documents "mirrors the usual approach commonly taken by airlines, both internationally and in India," and that there is no deadline or pressure to accept. The airline has paid an interim compensation of ₹25 lakh to families of 96 percent of the deceased. The Tata Group, which owns 75 percent of Air India, separately pledged ₹1 crore through a memorial trust, disbursed to 91 percent of families.

Boeing has been sued by family members in British courts. A final determination of what caused the crash — and who bears responsibility — remains months away.

## Why This Matters to the Diaspora

Flight AI171 was an Ahmedabad-to-London Gatwick service. Its passengers included NRI families traveling between India and the UK, business travelers, and students. The crash destroyed not just the aircraft but a Boeing 787-8 — the same type that flies dozens of Air India routes connecting India to Europe, North America, and the Gulf.

For diaspora families who fly these routes regularly, the probe's outcome will shape confidence in Air India's safety culture under Tata Group ownership. It will also determine whether the regulatory and maintenance frameworks that govern Indian aviation are adequate for the scale of air travel the country now handles.

The AAIB has said the purpose of the investigation is to improve aviation safety, not to apportion blame. But for the families of the 229 passengers, 12 crew members, and 19 people on the ground who died on June 12, 2025, the distinction offers little comfort. They want answers — and they want them before being asked to sign away their right to seek them.
